extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, dramatists, and readers/scholars of Restoration drama
extracted.subtask_description: Critical commentary on Dryden's comedy 'The Assignation' that identifies causes of its theatrical failure and extracts principles about what makes a stage-play (especially Restoration comedy) succeed or fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lameness of the action (plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author hints at the 'lameness of the action' as a cause of a play's failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A weak, ill-constructed, or 'lame' plot will predispose audiences to reject a piece; the author himself admits a defect of action. This is given as a primary reason for a play's poor reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared responsibility of poet and performers
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet and the performers are nearly equally involved in the disgrace of a condemned piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a play fails, blame may lie with both the author's text (plot, characterization) and the players' performance (delivery, taste). One should evaluate both writing and production when diagnosing theatrical failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid political or religious provocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles or content that suggest ridicule of public figures or religions (e.g., 'Love in a Nunnery') can arouse suspicion and audience condemnation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if not intended, associations with sensitive political or religious targets may prompt hostile reception; be cautious about titles, apparent targets, or ambiguous satire that could be interpreted as attacking powerful groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inelegant stage contrivances ('jeu de theatre')
rubrics_metrics.description: Absurd or vulgar theatrical tricks (example: a prince pretending a fit of the colic) are inelegant and liable to ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overwrought or buffoonish stage antics can undermine a play's dignity and invite parody (as 'The Rehearsal' ridiculed the colic scene). Stage devices should fit the tone and not appear vulgar or contrived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality resides in mode of treatment, not subject alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality consists in the mode of treating a subject, more than in the subject itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrowing plots or stock characters is less damaging if the playwright's handling, style, and treatment bring freshness; critics value novel treatment over mere novelty of subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of borrowing and perceptions of plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception of plagiarism or heavy appropriation invites critical censure and derision (examples: disputes around Ravenscroft and charges of 'plagiary').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even commonplace borrowing should be managed so as not to appear a dishonest or slavish imitation; distinctive treatment and transparent adaptation reduce accusations of theft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moralizing by example rather than dry didacticism
rubrics_metrics.description: To lead an audience to reformation, use examples drawn from the audience's world rather than 'dull morals, gravely writ.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epilogues or moral aims are more effective when shown through lively examples and recognizable situations, not heavy-handed sermons. Dull didacticism alienates 'men of easy phlegm.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in satire / measured exposure of faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Over-exposing characters' vices (e.g., stripping 'women's frailty to the waist') or excessively brutal satire may be poor taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A balanced, moderate satire that avoids gratuitous exposure is preferable; the author is criticized for neither fully stripping vice nor severely exposing men's faults, implying a need for judicious severity and self-awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer familiar, domestic settings and believable situations for comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Some critics argue that laying scenes 'at home' and using domestic mistakes (mistaken identities, lovers' mix-ups) can create better comedy than extravagant or foreign tableaux.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience engagement often increases with relatable, everyday settings and plausible comic situations; extravagant or exotic scenes must earn their place by contributing genuinely to entertainment or theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actors' execution, taste, and delivery crucial to reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Players' taste and the quality of their execution (acting, singing, dancing) materially affect whether a piece pleases or shames the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even a well-written play can fail if actors perform poorly or lack taste; conversely, good players can elevate material. Producers should ensure performers suit the tone and requirements of the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive foreign affectation as comic device
rubrics_metrics.description: Overuse of foreign words, mannerisms, or affected phrases (e.g., continual Frenchisms) can be ridiculous and distract from the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreignisms can provide comic colour but should be used sparingly and purposefully; prolonged affectation risks making characters ludicrous rather than amusing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain plot momentum and deliver on dramatic designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience response sours when promised designs or devices fall short; interruptions or failures in execution ('each design fell short') create dissatisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the plot moving and ensure setups have satisfying payoffs; avoid digressions or anticlimactic resolutions that make the audience feel cheated of the intended 'sport' of the play.
